patient_information: A 40-year-old man from Togo. No other past medical history, comorbidities, or allergies are mentioned.
chief_complaint: Changes in both eyes for 4 years, painless subcutaneous bumps for two decades, and intense itching.
history_of_present_illness: A 40-year-old man presents with a 4-year history of progressive changes in both eyes, without visual disturbances. He is concerned as he has observed similar ocular features in other villagers who subsequently became blind. For the past two decades, he has also developed painless bumps under his skin. Additionally, he suffers from intense itching of his skin, which is severe enough to keep him awake at night.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient has always lived in a village in the savannah of Togo, located near a fast-flowing river. He reports that small biting flies are common near the river. In his village, it is common for adults in each family to have turned completely blind after developing eye changes similar to his.
physical_exam: Physical examination reveals opacities in the cornea of both eyes. The skin appears atrophic in some areas with loss of elasticity, and there are multiple scratch marks. Multiple firm, non-tender subcutaneous nodules, measuring 1 to 3 cm in diameter, are palpable in various regions, especially over bony prominences such as the ribs, iliac crest, femoral trochanters, and on the head.
labs_and_diagnostics: No laboratory investigations were reported for this patient. The diagnosis was made on clinical grounds in a resource-limited setting. The text notes that definitive diagnosis can be made by demonstrating microfilariae of Onchocerca volvulus in skin snips, or by visualizing microfilariae in the anterior chamber of the eye and cornea via slit-lamp examination. Serological tests for IgG4 antibodies to O. volvulus antigens (like Ov16) are also recommended by the WHO in certain contexts.
differential_diagnosis: Onchocerciasis (river blindness) was the most likely diagnosis due to the clinical triad of ocular changes, itchy dermatitis, and subcutaneous nodules in a patient from an endemic region. Other considerations for the subcutaneous nodules included lipomas and cysticerci of Taenia solium. The pruritic dermatitis could also be caused by scabies, HIV-associated eruptions, Mansonella streptocerca infection, yaws, leprosy, or mycotic infections.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was treated with a single dose of ivermectin (150 μg/kg), which was repeated after 3 months and again after 1 year. He also received a course of doxycycline at 100 mg daily for 6 weeks.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis is onchocerciasis (river blindness), caused by the filarial nematode Onchocerca volvulus. The diagnosis was established based on the highly typical clinical presentation, including the triad of corneal opacities, chronic pruritic dermatitis with skin atrophy, and subcutaneous nodules. The patient's long-term residency in an endemic area in Togo, with known exposure to biting blackflies near a fast-flowing river, provided strong epidemiological confirmation.
